story: Nicholas Winton, Trevor Chadwick, Doreen Warriner and other volunteers helped children leave Czechoslovakia for Britain. USHMM gives the official rescued total as 669. Winton’s family exhibition says their largest planned transport, for 250 children, was due 1 September 1939 and was cancelled by German authorities after Germany invaded Poland. The project’s scrapbook helped bring the rescue work to public attention nearly fifty years later.
angle: The planned 250-child transport never left Prague, despite the earlier success of the rescue team.
topic: Nicholas Winton and the cancelled 1 September 1939 transport for 250 children

claims.claim: The rescue team planned a transport for 250 children that never left Prague.
Winton and colleagues organized the rescue effort; credit belongs to the team.
669 children are officially counted as having reached Britain through Winton’s efforts.
The largest planned transport was due 1 September 1939.
The transport was cancelled as Germany invaded Poland and borders closed.
The 1939 scrapbook helped bring the rescue work into public view in 1988; Winton himself sought a home for it in 1987.
A Winton memorial honoring his rescue work stands at Prague Main Station; the Commons photograph dates to 2015.

disputed: Do not say the 250 children had boarded; the family exhibition calls the transport planned and cancelled, while a BBC retrospective used more definite wording.

Do not give a precise survival count for the cancelled transport. The family exhibition says nearly all are thought to have been sent to camps, but the individual fates are not established in the sources read.
Do not say the scrapbook was a secret from Winton’s wife for fifty years: he was seeking a home for it in 1987, and USHMM says Grete found it in 1988.
